title: Country Risk: When the Country Becomes a Party to Your Deal
summary: Investing across a border adds risks that no amount of good construction can remove: the currency can fall, money can become impossible to convert or send home, and the state can take or squeeze the asset. Learn the five country risks, and the three tools that manage them: matching, hedging and insurance.
body:
When you invest across a border, the host country becomes a silent party to every contract you sign. Its currency, its central bank and its government can change your returns more than your tenants or your contractor ever will, so you name those risks, measure them and decide in advance who carries each one.

Recall

Q. What is a direct agreement in project finance?

A. A contract among the lender, the project company and a key counterparty, giving the lender notice before termination, time to cure, and the right to step in and pass the contract to a new owner.

Q. In a condo pre-sale, what is buyer default?

A. A buyer's failure to complete the purchase at closing. The remedies, such as keeping the deposit or suing for the shortfall on resale, depend on the contract and local law.

Q. What does a corporate resolution do?

A. It records a decision of the board or shareholders, such as approving a loan or naming who may sign, and is the evidence that the company, not just an individual, made the decision.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you think across two systems, Canada and Guyana, and wealth that crosses a border carries risks a domestic developer never meets. A building can be well designed, well built and fully leased and still lose half its value to its owner in a year, measured in the currency the owner spends. Lenders, insurers and development finance institutions price these risks precisely. If you cannot name them, you will pay their price without knowing what you are paying for.

The five country risks

In plain English: five things can go wrong because of where the project is, not what the project is.

First, currency mismatch: earning in one currency and owing in another. If your rents are in local currency and your loan is in United States dollars, a fall in the local currency raises your debt in local terms while your income stays where it was. Second, convertibility risk: you have local currency but cannot legally exchange it for the foreign currency you need, because the central bank restricts conversion. Third, transfer risk: you can convert, but you cannot send the money out of the country. Lenders often group the second and third together as convertibility and transfer risk. Fourth, expropriation: the state takes the asset outright, or takes its value step by step through measures such as cancelled permits, frozen rents or confiscatory taxes, which practitioners call creeping expropriation. Fifth, political violence and breach of contract by the state: war, civil disturbance or a government refusing to honour an agreement it signed.

The first is a market risk; it happens without anyone acting against you. The other four are political: they happen because a government decides something. That distinction matters because they are managed with different tools.

Tool one: match the currencies

The cleanest control for currency mismatch is not to have one. If the project earns local currency, borrow in local currency. If the project earns dollars, for instance a hotel pricing rooms in dollars to foreign visitors, dollar debt may be a reasonable match. Practitioners call this a natural hedge: the income and the obligation move together, so a currency move hurts both sides of the ledger equally.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A local exchange rate of 100 local currency units to one dollar. The project earns 500,000,000 local units a year, 5,000,000 dollars. It owes 3,500,000 dollars a year on a dollar loan, so coverage is about 1.43. The local currency falls to 150 units per dollar. Rents have not moved, so the same 500,000,000 units are now worth about 3,333,000 dollars, and coverage falls to about 0.95. The building has not changed. The loan is in default territory. Had the loan been in local currency, the fall would not have touched coverage at all.

Say that out loud now.

Earn and owe in the same currency, or know exactly what a fall costs me.

Tool two: hedge what you cannot match

Local currency debt is often unavailable, short-term or expensive in smaller markets. Then the sponsor can hedge: use a contract that fixes an exchange rate in advance. A forward contract locks a rate for a future date; a cross-currency swap exchanges payments in one currency for payments in another over the life of a loan. The price of a hedge reflects the difference between the two countries' interest rates. That has a consequence beginners miss: hedging dollar debt back into local currency usually costs about what borrowing locally would have cost. There is no free money in borrowing in the cheaper currency. And hedges for long tenors in small currencies may not exist at all, which leaves a gap between a 15-year loan and a hedge you can buy for one or two years.

Tool three: insure the political risks

The political risks can be insured. Political-risk insurance covers losses from currency inconvertibility and transfer restriction, expropriation, political violence and, in some policies, a government's breach of contract. It is sold by private insurers and by public bodies; the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency, part of the World Bank Group, is the best-known public provider. Many governments also run export credit or investment agencies that insure their own nationals' foreign investments. Policies carry waiting periods, exclusions and conditions, and they do not cover ordinary currency depreciation. That point bears repeating: political-risk insurance pays when you cannot convert or transfer, not when the rate is merely worse.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A sponsor has 10,000,000 dollars of equity in a project abroad. Distributions of 800,000 dollars a year are blocked when the central bank stops releasing foreign currency. With convertibility and transfer cover, after the policy's waiting period the insurer pays the dollar value of the blocked amount, at the rate before the restriction, and takes the local currency in exchange. Without cover, the sponsor waits, perhaps for years, with cash it cannot use.

How the best do it

The most experienced cross-border investors decide currency strategy before they choose a lender, not after. They map, line by line, which currency each revenue and each cost is paid in, size debt in the revenue currency where they can, hedge the gap for as long as the market allows, and insure the political risks for the full tenor of their equity. Development finance institutions increasingly offer local currency loans for exactly this reason. A small developer can copy this with a two-column page: every cash flow, its currency, and who carries the risk if that currency moves.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: exchange gains and losses, and hedge payments, may be taxed differently from operating income; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a guarantee in dollars on a local currency project carries the mismatch onto your personal balance sheet. Banking: confirm early that your bank can convert and move funds out, and how fast. Governance: the board should approve currency exposure as a deliberate decision, with limits. Estate: assets in another currency and country change in value to your heirs as the rate moves. Exit: a sale price in local currency is worth only what you can convert and transfer on the day.

Professional sign-off required: lawyer and financial adviser familiar with the host country's foreign exchange rules; insurance broker, on political-risk cover.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is borrowing in a foreign currency because it is cheaper, without recognising that the lower rate is the market's price for the currency risk you have just taken on. The control is to model a severe depreciation before signing and to approve the exposure in writing.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes political-risk insurance protects against a falling currency. It does not. It protects against being unable to convert or transfer, and against acts of the state.

Callback

In Week 22, Elias taught residence versus source: who taxes you depends on where you live and where the income arises. Country risk is the same map seen through a different lens. Where the income arises decides not only who taxes it, but whose currency it is paid in and whose central bank decides whether you can take it home.

Recap

Country risk has five parts: currency mismatch, convertibility, transfer, expropriation and political violence or breach. Match currencies where you can, hedge what you cannot, and insure the political risks, knowing that insurance does not cover ordinary depreciation and hedges cost roughly the interest difference.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: Argentina's convertibility collapse of 2001 and 2002.
checklist: I can name the five country risks and say which are market and which are political.
I have mapped every cash flow in the project by currency.
Where possible, my debt is in the currency the project earns.
I have modelled coverage after a severe currency fall.
I know what a hedge costs and how long a tenor the market offers.
I know what political-risk insurance covers and that it excludes ordinary depreciation.
My board has approved any currency exposure in writing, with a limit.
I have confirmed how my bank converts and transfers funds out of the country.
head: Field checklist
speak: Investing across a border makes the host country a silent party to every contract. There are five country risks. Currency mismatch: earning in one currency and owing in another. Convertibility: being unable to exchange local money for foreign. Transfer: being unable to send it out. Expropriation: the state taking the asset, outright or step by step. And political violence or a government breaking its contract. Three tools manage them. Match currencies, so a project earning local money borrows local money. Hedge what I cannot match, knowing a hedge costs roughly the interest rate difference, so borrowing in the cheaper currency is not free. And insure the political risks, knowing political-risk insurance pays when I cannot convert or transfer, not when the rate is simply worse. In my example, a fall from 100 to 150 units per dollar took coverage from 1.43 to 0.95 with no change in the building. So I model the severe case before I sign.
terms: Currency mismatch — earning income in one currency while owing debt or costs in another, so exchange rate moves change your ability to pay.
Convertibility and transfer risk — the risk that you cannot legally exchange local currency for foreign currency, or cannot send it out of the country.
Political-risk insurance — cover against losses from inconvertibility, transfer restriction, expropriation, political violence and sometimes a state's breach of contract.

hostile.q: Your rents are in local currency and you want a dollar loan. What happens to my coverage if the currency falls by a third?
hostile.a: On our base numbers it falls from about 1.43 to about 0.95, which is below one, so I am not asking you to take that risk unprotected. Either we borrow part of the debt in local currency, or we hedge the dollar debt for as long as the market allows and hold a currency reserve for the rest, or we price rent escalations in the leases. I have modelled all three and will show you coverage under each at the severe rate.

title: Argentina 2001 to 2002: When the Peg Broke and the Contracts Changed
summary: For a decade Argentina fixed its peso at one to one with the United States dollar, and dollar contracts became normal. When the peg broke in early 2002, the peso fell sharply, deposits were frozen and many dollar contracts were converted into pesos by law. Roman joins Ford to show how currency, convertibility and contract risk arrived together.
rule: Rule 43: Never borrow in a currency your project does not earn unless the mismatch is hedged or reserved against, sized to survive a severe devaluation, and approved in writing as a deliberate decision, because a peg is a policy and policies end.
body:
Argentina's currency board held the peso at one to one with the dollar for about ten years, long enough for people to treat a policy as a law of nature. When it broke in early 2002, the currency risk, the convertibility risk and the contract risk all arrived in the same few weeks.

Recall

Q. What is a natural hedge?

A. Matching the currency of income and obligations, for example borrowing in the currency the project earns, so an exchange rate move affects both sides equally.

Q. What does a pre-sale threshold protect for a construction lender?

A. Evidence of demand and a base of committed revenue, so the lender is not funding a building the market may not buy. The threshold is set by commercial practice, loan by loan.

Q. What is signing authority in a company?

A. The power, granted by the company's resolutions or by-laws, for named people to bind the company in contracts, cheques or filings, often with limits and dual-signature rules.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me because this is the textbook case of every country risk Roman listed yesterday arriving together. It is not a story about one developer. It is a story about a whole economy that borrowed, priced and contracted in a currency it did not control. The general facts below are widely documented; I avoid precise exchange rates and amounts I cannot confirm.

1. Timeline

In 1991 Argentina adopted a convertibility system that fixed the peso at one to one with the United States dollar, backed by foreign reserves. Inflation, which had been severe, fell, and confidence returned. Over the 1990s, dollar deposits, dollar loans and dollar-linked contracts became common, including mortgages and utility tariffs. From the late 1990s the economy entered a long recession, public debt grew and the fixed rate became harder to defend. During 2001 depositors withdrew funds. In December 2001 the government restricted cash withdrawals from banks, a measure known as the corralito. Unrest followed, the president resigned, and the government declared a default on much of its public debt. In January 2002 the fixed rate was abandoned, and the peso lost most of its value against the dollar during 2002. Many dollar-denominated contracts, deposits and loans were converted into pesos by government measures, a process called pesification, at rates the government set.

2. Key decisions

Three kinds of decision built the exposure. Borrowers chose dollar loans because dollar rates were lower than peso rates. Lenders and investors chose to treat dollar contracts inside Argentina as if they were dollar risk, not Argentine risk. And foreign investors in utilities and infrastructure accepted tariffs set in dollars but collected in pesos, inside Argentina's legal system.

3. Assumptions

The governing assumption was that the peg would hold, or, if it broke, that dollar contracts would be honoured in dollars. The second assumption was the one that failed most completely. A contract written in dollars but governed by local law and enforced by local courts is a contract the local state can change.

Say that out loud now.

A dollar contract under local law is local risk wearing a dollar sign.

4. Incentives

The lower rate on dollar loans rewarded borrowers for taking currency risk, and they did not price the risk because the peg made it invisible. Banks earned the spread on dollar lending. Governments benefited from the confidence the peg created and had reasons to defend it longer than was wise.

5. Warning signs ignored

A recession lasting years, rising public debt, a fixed rate that made exports less competitive, falling reserves and deposits leaving the banks were all visible before December 2001. Each was a signal that the policy holding the peso was under strain. Investors who treated the peg as permanent read these signals as noise.

6. Point of no return

For a borrower with a dollar loan and peso income, the point of no return was not January 2002. It was the day the loan was signed without a plan for the peg breaking. After that, the borrower's fate depended on a government decision he could not influence.

7. Root cause

Roman's reading is that the root cause was confusing a policy with a property of the world. A fixed exchange rate is a choice a government makes and can unmake. Every contract priced on the assumption that it could not end carried a hidden option, held by the state, to change the terms.

What it means for a developer

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers in a hypothetical pegged economy. A developer finances an apartment building with a 20,000,000 dollar loan at 6 percent while local currency loans cost 10 percent. Rents are 2,400,000 dollars a year equivalent, collected in local currency at one to one. Interest is 1,200,000 dollars, so interest coverage is 2.0. The peg breaks and the local currency falls to three units per dollar. Rents, frozen by law for a year, are still 2,400,000 local units, now worth 800,000 dollars. Interest is still 1,200,000 dollars. Coverage is about 0.67. The developer saved 800,000 dollars a year of interest for some years and then lost the building.

A second example. The same developer, borrowing the 20,000,000 in local currency at 10 percent, pays 2,000,000 local units of interest, coverage 1.2. After the break, rents and interest are both in local units, and coverage is still 1.2. The return measured in dollars has fallen, which hurts, but the developer still owns the building. That is the difference between a loss and a ruin.

The other lesson: treaties and arbitration

Many foreign investors whose contracts were changed brought claims against Argentina under bilateral investment treaties, agreements between two states that protect each other's investors, often before international arbitration bodies. These claims took years. Treaty protection is real, but it is slow, uncertain and no substitute for a structure that survives the event. Day 4 takes it further.

The prevention habit

Roman's prevention habit is a peg question asked at every investment committee in a country with a fixed or tightly managed currency. Three parts. What would our coverage, loan to value and equity be worth the week after the rate is released and falls by half? Which of our contracts are governed by local law, so the state could convert or freeze them? And what is our plan for the first ninety days: which payments stop, which cash is protected, and who decides? If the committee cannot answer all three, the deal is not ready.

The habit costs one page and one hour. It also changes behaviour quietly. A team that has written down the ninety-day plan tends to keep more cash outside the country, keep its records outside the country, and prefer local debt even when it is dearer. Those are exactly the choices that separated survivors from casualties in 2002.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is taking the cheaper foreign-currency loan because the exchange rate has been stable for years. Stability is evidence that the policy is working, not that it is permanent. The control is to model a break in the peg and to size equity, reserves and hedges to survive it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner believes that writing the contract in dollars protects him. It protects him only if the contract is governed by a law and enforced in a forum that the host state cannot change, and even then collection is slow.

Callback

In Week 27, Remi taught cycles: supply, credit, interest rates and timing. Argentina shows a currency cycle running beneath the property cycle, long and quiet, then very fast. A developer who reads only the property cycle can be right about demand and still be ruined by the currency.

Recap

Argentina's peg made dollar contracts feel safe for a decade. When it broke in early 2002, the currency fell, deposits were frozen and many dollar contracts were converted into pesos. The root cause was treating a policy as permanent. Rule 43 makes the mismatch a deliberate, sized and approved decision.

Next: Roman, on The Money: what currency risk does to coverage, value and return, and what hedges and insurance really cost.
checklist: I treat any fixed or managed exchange rate as a policy that can end.
I have modelled a break in the peg and its effect on coverage.
I know which law governs my currency-denominated contracts and where they are enforced.
I compare the interest saved by foreign borrowing with the loss in a severe devaluation.
I hold equity, reserves or hedges sized to survive the severe case.
I know whether a bilateral investment treaty covers my investment and how slow a claim would be.
Any currency mismatch is approved in writing as a deliberate decision.
I have written Rule 43 in my decision journal.
head: Field checklist
speak: From 1991 Argentina fixed its peso at one to one with the dollar, and for a decade dollar loans, deposits and contracts became normal. After a long recession and growing public debt, deposits drained, the government restricted withdrawals in December 2001 and defaulted on much of its debt, and in January 2002 the peg was abandoned. The peso lost most of its value during 2002, and many dollar contracts were converted into pesos by law. The root cause was treating a policy as permanent. A dollar contract under local law is local risk wearing a dollar sign. In my hypothetical example, a borrower who saved interest with a dollar loan saw coverage fall from 2.0 to about 0.67 when the currency fell to a third of its value, while the borrower in local currency kept coverage at 1.2 and kept the building. Rule 43: never borrow in a currency the project does not earn unless the mismatch is hedged, sized and approved in writing.
terms: Currency board — a system that fixes the local currency to a foreign currency at a set rate, backed by foreign reserves.
Pesification — Argentina's 2002 conversion, by government measures, of many dollar-denominated contracts and balances into pesos at set rates.
Bilateral investment treaty — an agreement between two states protecting each other's investors, often with access to international arbitration.

hostile.q: The exchange rate here has not moved in twelve years. Why are you paying for local currency debt at a higher rate?
hostile.a: Because twelve years of stability tells me the policy is working, not that it cannot end. The extra interest is the price of not losing the building if it does. I have modelled a fall to a third of the current value: with dollar debt our coverage goes well below one, and with local debt it stays above one. I would rather earn a lower dollar return in a bad year than lose the asset.

title: What Currency Risk Does to Coverage, Value and Return
summary: A currency fall hits a cross-border project three times: in coverage, in loan to value and in the return measured in your home currency. Hedges and insurance reduce the damage, and both have a price. Learn to put the three hits and the two prices on one page.
body:
A fall in the local currency hits a cross-border project three times: it weakens coverage on foreign debt, it raises loan to value in the lender's currency, and it cuts the return you take home. Hedges and insurance blunt those hits at a price, and you choose them by comparing the price with the damage.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause in the Argentina case?

A. Treating a fixed exchange rate, which is a government policy, as permanent, so contracts priced on it carried a hidden option for the state to change their terms.

Q. In a condo project, what is deposit insurance?

A. Cover, provided by an insurer or a statutory scheme, that protects buyers' deposits if the developer fails. Whether it exists and how it works depends on the jurisdiction.

Q. What is a minute book?

A. The company's official record of its constitution, resolutions, directors, officers and share registers, kept as evidence of how decisions were made.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the money you spend, save and leave to your family is counted in one currency. A project in another currency can look healthy in its own books while your real wealth shrinks. Lenders count in their currency too, and they will act on the hit to coverage or loan to value long before you feel the hit to your return. You need all three numbers, and the price of protecting each.

The three hits

Take a hypothetical project in a country whose currency trades at 100 local units to the dollar. Net operating income is 500,000,000 local units, 5,000,000 dollars. The project is valued at an 8 percent capitalisation rate in local terms: 500,000,000 divided by 0.08 is 6,250,000,000 local units, 62,500,000 dollars. A dollar loan of 40,000,000 dollars costs 3,500,000 dollars a year.

Now the currency falls to 150 units per dollar. Hit one, coverage: income in dollars falls to about 3,333,000, and coverage falls from about 1.43 to about 0.95. Hit two, loan to value: the building is still worth 6,250,000,000 local units, but in dollars that is about 41,700,000. The loan is 40,000,000. Loan to value rises from 64 percent to 96 percent, so the lender is almost uncovered. Hit three, your return: your equity, 22,500,000 dollars at the start, is now worth about 1,700,000 dollars on paper, and your distributions in dollars are close to zero because the debt service consumes them.

The building did not lose a tenant or a dollar of maintenance. Every one of those losses is currency.

Say that out loud now.

A currency fall hits coverage, loan to value and my return, and the lender acts on the first two.

The price of a hedge

In plain English: to fix tomorrow's exchange rate today, you pay about the difference between the two countries' interest rates.

The professional framing is that a forward exchange rate equals today's rate adjusted for the interest rate difference between the two currencies, a relationship economists call covered interest parity. A worked example, hypothetical. Local interest rates are 12 percent and dollar rates 5 percent. Today's rate is 100. The one-year forward rate is about 100 times 1.12 divided by 1.05, about 106.7 units per dollar. If you lock in next year's income at that rate, 500,000,000 units buy about 4,690,000 dollars, not 5,000,000. Coverage on the dollar loan becomes about 1.34. That 310,000 dollar shortfall against today's rate is the hedge's real cost, and it is roughly what you saved by borrowing in dollars rather than locally. The hedge does not make the currency risk vanish; it converts it into a known cost.

Two more facts about hedges. In smaller currencies the market may offer them only for a year or two, so a long loan stays partly unhedged. And a hedge that is losing money may require you to post cash as collateral, which can drain liquidity exactly when the currency is under strain.

The price of insurance

Political-risk insurance is priced as an annual premium on the amount insured, varying with country, cover and term. As a purely hypothetical illustration, at 1 percent a year, insuring 10,000,000 dollars of equity against inconvertibility, transfer restriction and expropriation costs 100,000 dollars a year. Compare that with the loss it covers. If you estimate a 2 percent annual chance of a transfer restriction that would block 800,000 dollars of distributions for three years, the expected annual loss is 2 percent of 2,400,000, about 48,000 dollars, plus the far larger risk of expropriation. Insurance is rarely justified by expected loss alone; it is justified by the losses you cannot survive. Remember that it covers none of the three hits above, which come from ordinary depreciation.

Putting it on one page

Roman's page has four rows: unhedged, hedged for one year, local currency debt, and partial local debt with a currency reserve. For each row, show coverage and loan to value at today's rate and at a severe rate, the dollar return to equity in each case, and the annual cost of the protection. The answer is a choice, not a formula, but the page makes it a choice you made deliberately.

How a lender reads the same page

A worked example of the lender's view, hypothetical. A lender with a 40,000,000 dollar loan and a covenant of 75 percent loan to value, tested in dollars, sees the severe column at 96 percent. Under a typical covenant, that triggers a demand to repay the loan down to 75 percent, which here means paying about 8,750,000 dollars, or posting that much in cash collateral. The arithmetic: 75 percent of about 41,670,000 is about 31,250,000, so the excess is 40,000,000 less 31,250,000. Few sponsors hold that much spare cash in the middle of a currency crisis, when every other investor is also selling. Covenant terms are commercial practice and vary; your loan agreement decides what is tested and how it is cured.

Now the same lender looking at strategy B, local currency debt: loan to value is still 64 percent in local terms, because the loan and the building are in the same currency. Nothing is triggered. This is why some lenders prefer to lend in local currency where they can fund it, and why development finance institutions value local currency lending so highly.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's note. Your personal balance sheet should show assets and liabilities by currency, not only by amount. If your future spending, your family's needs and your guarantees are in one currency, a large share of assets in another is a currency position, whether you meant to take it or not. Many families keep a reserve in the currency of their future spending so that a fall in an investment currency never forces a sale at the worst time. This is conceptual; a licensed adviser is required before you act.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is watching coverage in local currency while the lender watches loan to value in dollars, and learning of the breach from the lender. The control is to report every covenant in the currency the lender tests it in, every month.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner thinks a hedge is a profit opportunity or a loss to be avoided. It is neither. It is a known cost paid to remove an unknown one, and it should be judged by the damage it prevents, not by whether it made or lost money this quarter.

Callback

In Week 36, Priya taught loan to value, loan to cost and fixed versus floating rates, and that hedges exist for interest rates. Currency hedges are the same idea in a different dimension: you pay a known price to turn a variable you cannot control into one you can plan around.

Recap

A currency fall hits coverage, loan to value and your home-currency return. A forward hedge costs roughly the interest rate difference and is often available only for short tenors. Political-risk insurance covers acts of the state, not depreciation. Put all four strategies on one page, at today's and a severe rate.

Next: REGA, on The Rules: foreign exchange law, investment treaties, stabilisation clauses and how Canada and Guyana approach them.
checklist: I compute coverage, loan to value and home-currency return at a severe exchange rate.
I know which covenants my lender tests in which currency.
I can estimate a forward rate from the two interest rates.
I know how long a hedge tenor the market offers in my currency.
I know whether a hedge could require me to post collateral.
I compare insurance premiums with the losses I could not survive, not only expected loss.
My personal balance sheet shows assets and liabilities by currency.
head: Field checklist
speak: A fall in the local currency hits a cross-border project three times. In my example, the currency goes from 100 to 150 units per dollar. Coverage on a dollar loan falls from about 1.43 to 0.95. Loan to value in dollars rises from 64 percent to 96 percent, so the lender is nearly uncovered. And my equity in dollars almost disappears. Not one tenant left; it is all currency. A forward hedge fixes the rate, but its price is roughly the interest rate difference: at 12 percent local and 5 percent dollar rates, next year's rate is about 106.7, which costs me about what I saved by borrowing dollars. Hedges in small currencies are often short and may require collateral. Political-risk insurance covers inconvertibility, transfer and expropriation, not ordinary depreciation. So I put four strategies on one page at today's rate and a severe rate, and choose deliberately.
terms: Forward rate — an exchange rate agreed today for a transaction on a future date.
Covered interest parity — the relationship by which a forward exchange rate reflects the interest rate difference between two currencies.
Loan to value in the lender's currency — the loan divided by the asset's value converted into the currency the loan is denominated in.

hostile.q: You hedged one year of income. My loan is fifteen years. What protects me in years two to fifteen?
hostile.a: Three things. We roll the hedge each year for as long as the market offers it, and the model assumes the cost rises. We hold a currency reserve funded from early distributions, sized to cover debt service for twelve months at a severe rate. And a third of the debt is in local currency, so part of the payment moves with income. I will show you coverage in years two to fifteen at the severe rate under that structure.

title: Foreign Exchange Law, Investment Treaties and Stabilisation Clauses
summary: Country risk is governed by three bodies of rules: the host state's foreign exchange and investment law, the contracts you sign with the state, and the treaties between states. Learn what each can and cannot promise, how political-risk insurance conditions work, and how Canada and Guyana approach the point in general terms.
body:
The rules that govern country risk come in three layers: the host state's own foreign exchange and investment law, the contracts you sign with that state, and the treaties between states. Each layer protects you differently, and the outer layers are slower and narrower than most investors assume.

Recall

Q. What three hits does a currency fall cause?

A. It weakens coverage on foreign-currency debt, raises loan to value in the lender's currency, and cuts the return measured in the investor's home currency.

Q. Why does a construction lender care about buyers' deposits in a pre-sale project?

A. Because deposits show commitment and may fund part of the cost, and because the rules on whether they can be used before completion affect how much equity the lender requires.

Q. Why does the choice of vehicle matter before a deal starts?

A. Because the vehicle decides liability, tax treatment, governance and how easily the project can be financed or sold, and changing it later can be costly or taxable.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, every promise a government makes to an investor sits somewhere in these three layers. When an investor says "we are protected", the right question is "by which layer, enforced where, and how quickly?" I teach concepts and how to think. Every rule mentioned here varies by country and changes over time; verify it against the primary source before you rely on it.

Layer one: the host state's own law

In plain English: the country's own laws say whether you may change and send money, and what an investor is promised.

The professional framing has two parts. Foreign exchange law, usually administered by the central bank, governs whether residents and foreigners may buy and sell foreign currency, through which licensed dealers, and whether payments abroad need approval or registration. Some countries have no general controls in normal times; others require approvals for large transfers, or register foreign investment so that its return can later be repatriated. Investment law, sometimes a specific investment act, may promise national treatment, compensation for expropriation, or the right to repatriate profits. Its weakness is obvious: what one parliament enacts, another can amend.

A worked example, hypothetical. A foreign investor brings 5,000,000 dollars into a country that requires foreign investment to be registered with the central bank to secure the right to repatriate it. The investor's lawyer files the registration on arrival. Years later, controls tighten, and only registered capital and its declared returns may leave. A second investor, who skipped the registration because it seemed like paperwork, finds his capital in the queue behind everyone who filed. The rule was not hidden; it was ignored.

Layer two: contracts with the state

When a project is large or strategic, the investor may sign an agreement directly with the government: a concession, a development agreement or an investment agreement. Such agreements may contain a stabilisation clause, a promise that changes in law after signing will not apply to the project, or that the investor will be compensated if they do. They may also choose a governing law and an international arbitration forum. The protection is stronger than domestic law alone, but a state that breaches its own contract is exactly the risk you are worried about, and enforcing an award against a state's assets is its own long project.

Say that out loud now.

Domestic law can be amended, a state contract can be breached, and a treaty claim takes years.

Layer three: treaties between states

A bilateral investment treaty is an agreement between two states protecting each other's investors. Typical protections include fair and equitable treatment, compensation for expropriation, free transfer of funds subject to stated exceptions, and the right to bring a claim against the host state in international arbitration. The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, part of the World Bank Group, is one forum that hears such claims. Whether you are protected depends on whether a treaty exists between the host state and the state of your investing entity, how the treaty defines investor and investment, and whether your structure meets those definitions. Treaties can also be terminated, and many have survival periods after termination. Read the actual treaty text.

A second worked example, hypothetical. An investor in a state with no treaty with his home country holds the project through a company in a third state that does have a treaty. If the structure was set up for genuine business reasons before any dispute, it may qualify; if it was created after a dispute was foreseeable, tribunals have refused jurisdiction. Structure for protection early, and for real reasons, or it may not hold. Professional sign-off required: international arbitration lawyer.

Insurance conditions

Political-risk insurance policies add their own rules. Most carry a waiting period, such as several months of continuous inconvertibility before a claim is paid. Most exclude losses caused by the investor's own breach of local law, and losses from currency depreciation. Most require the investor to pursue local remedies and to cooperate with the insurer, which on payment takes over the investor's claim against the state, a right called subrogation. Read the definition of each covered event; an expropriation policy that covers only outright seizure may not respond to a slow squeeze.

Two Systems: Canada and Guyana

This is a conceptual comparison in general terms; verify every point against the primary source before relying on it. Canada's dollar floats, and in normal times Canada does not impose general controls on converting or sending funds, though anti-money-laundering reporting and foreign investment review rules apply in defined cases. Guyana has its own currency, administered by its central bank, and foreign exchange is bought and sold through licensed dealers; an investor should confirm with local counsel and the central bank how conversion and repatriation work in practice, what documentation banks require, and whether any registration helps secure later transfers. On treaties, both countries participate in international investment arrangements, and whether a specific treaty protects a specific investor depends on the treaty text and the investor's structure. The habit to keep is the same in both systems: ask the bank, before you invest, exactly what it needs to convert and send your money out, and get the answer in writing.

Building the protection map

Put the three layers and the insurance on one table. Rows are the country risks: mismatch, convertibility, transfer, expropriation, political violence, state breach. Columns are domestic law, state contract, treaty, insurance and structure. In each cell write what protects you, where it would be enforced, and how long recovery would take. Most investors who build this table find two things. Mismatch is covered by nothing except structure, because no law or policy protects you against a falling rate. And the cells with the strongest legal protection usually have the longest recovery time, measured in years. That is the reason structure does most of the work, and law is the backstop.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is relying on a protection in the wrong layer, for example a treaty that does not cover your structure, or an insurance policy whose waiting period outlasts your loan's cure period. The control is a protection map: each country risk, the layer that covers it, the forum, the conditions and the time to recovery.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats registration and documentation requirements as bureaucracy to minimise. In exchange control systems, the documents are the right to take your money home.

Callback

In Week 19, LEX taught sources of law: statute, regulation, contract and precedent, and how courts rank them. Country risk adds two sources above the domestic courts, the state contract and the treaty, and shows that a protection is only as good as the forum that will enforce it.

Recap

Domestic foreign exchange and investment law can be amended. Contracts with the state may stabilise the law and choose arbitration, but the state can breach them. Treaties protect qualifying investors in international arbitration, slowly. Insurance has waiting periods, exclusions and subrogation. Map each risk to its layer before you invest.

Next: Roman, on The Numbers: a currency stress worked step by step, unhedged, hedged and in local currency.
checklist: I know the host country's foreign exchange rules and who administers them.
I have completed any registration that secures the right to repatriate capital and returns.
I know whether a stabilisation clause or state contract applies to my project.
I have read the text of any investment treaty I may rely on.
My holding structure was set up for real business reasons before any dispute.
I know my insurance policy's waiting periods, exclusions and subrogation terms.
I have a protection map of each country risk, its layer, forum and time to recovery.
I have the bank's conversion and transfer requirements in writing.
head: Field checklist
speak: Country risk is governed in three layers. First, the host state's own law: foreign exchange rules, usually run by the central bank, and investment law that may promise repatriation or compensation, but what one parliament enacts another can amend. Second, contracts with the state, which may include a stabilisation clause shielding the project from later changes in law and may choose international arbitration, but the state can still breach them. Third, treaties between states, which protect qualifying investors and allow claims in international arbitration, slowly, and only if my structure meets the treaty's definitions and was set up for real reasons before any dispute. Political-risk insurance adds waiting periods, exclusions and subrogation. In Canada the dollar floats with no general controls in normal times; in Guyana, foreign exchange runs through licensed dealers under the central bank, so I confirm the process with local counsel and the bank in writing.
terms: Stabilisation clause — a term in a state contract promising that later changes in law will not apply to the project, or that the investor will be compensated if they do.
Repatriation — converting and sending profits or capital from the host country back to the investor.
Subrogation — the insurer's right, after paying a claim, to take over the insured's claim against the party that caused the loss.

hostile.q: You say the investment treaty protects you. Your holding company was formed eight months ago. Why would a tribunal accept jurisdiction?
hostile.a: I would not rely on it if the company had been formed to manufacture a claim. It was formed before we signed the land contract, for financing and governance reasons recorded in the minute book at the time, and it holds real staff and decisions. Even so, I treat the treaty as a last resort that takes years. My first line is the structure: local currency debt, registration of the capital with the central bank, and political-risk insurance with a waiting period shorter than our loan's cure period.

title: A Currency Stress, Worked Step by Step
summary: One project, four financing strategies, two exchange rates. Work through coverage, loan to value and the home-currency return for each, and see which strategy survives a severe devaluation and what it costs in a normal year. All numbers are hypothetical.
body:
Run one hypothetical project through four financing strategies at today's exchange rate and at a severe one, and the choice stops being a matter of opinion: you can see what each strategy earns in a normal year and what it costs in a bad one.

Recall

Q. What is a stabilisation clause?

A. A term in a contract with the state promising that later changes in law will not apply to the project, or that the investor will be compensated if they do.

Q. What is the in-balance test?

A. At each draw, the undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the full cost to complete, or the borrower deposits the shortfall.

Q. What is a shareholders' resolution, as distinct from a directors' resolution?

A. A decision taken by the owners of the company, usually on fundamental matters such as amending the constitution or approving a sale of the business, while directors' resolutions cover management decisions.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, cross-border financing choices are often made on the interest rate because the rate is the only number on the term sheet. Today you will make the currency risk a number too. All figures are hypothetical, in a hypothetical country whose currency we call local units.

The facts

Today's exchange rate is 100 local units to the dollar. The building earns net operating income of 500,000,000 local units a year, 5,000,000 dollars. It is valued at an 8 percent capitalisation rate in local terms, 6,250,000,000 local units, 62,500,000 dollars. You need to borrow the equivalent of 40,000,000 dollars. Dollar debt costs 3,500,000 dollars a year in debt service. Local currency debt of the same size, 4,000,000,000 local units, costs 380,000,000 local units a year, because local interest rates are higher. The severe case is a fall to 150 local units per dollar within a year, with rents unable to rise for twelve months.

Step 1: strategy A, unhedged dollar debt

Today: coverage is 5,000,000 divided by 3,500,000, about 1.43. Severe: income is 500,000,000 divided by 150, about 3,333,000 dollars; coverage about 0.95. Loan to value in dollars goes from 40,000,000 over 62,500,000, 64 percent, to 40,000,000 over about 41,700,000, 96 percent. Cash after debt service in a normal year is 1,500,000 dollars; in the severe year it is negative, about minus 167,000 dollars.

Step 2: strategy B, local currency debt

Today: coverage is 500,000,000 over 380,000,000, about 1.32. Severe: income and debt service are both in local units, so coverage stays about 1.32. Loan to value in local terms stays at 64 percent. Cash after debt service is 120,000,000 local units, which is 1,200,000 dollars today and 800,000 dollars at the severe rate. The dollar return falls, but there is no breach.

Say that out loud now.

Unhedged, I earn more in a normal year and breach in a bad one; in local currency, I earn less and survive.

Step 3: strategy C, dollar debt with a one-year hedge

Local rates are 12 percent and dollar rates 5 percent, so the one-year forward rate is about 100 times 1.12 over 1.05, about 106.7. Lock in the year's income at that rate: 500,000,000 over 106.7 is about 4,690,000 dollars. Coverage is about 1.34 whatever happens to the spot rate during the year. Normal-year cash after debt service is about 1,190,000 dollars, close to strategy B. But the hedge covers one year. If the currency falls in year one and you roll the hedge at the new, lower level, year two's income in dollars is set near the severe rate, and coverage falls towards 0.95 again. The hedge buys time, not immunity.

Step 4: strategy D, half local, half dollar, with a reserve

Borrow 20,000,000 dollars in dollars, 1,750,000 dollars of debt service, and the equivalent of 20,000,000 dollars in local units, 190,000,000 local units of debt service. Fund a currency reserve of 1,000,000 dollars from equity. Today: total debt service in local terms is 175,000,000 plus 190,000,000, 365,000,000 local units; coverage about 1.37. Severe: dollar debt service becomes 262,500,000 local units, plus 190,000,000, total 452,500,000; coverage about 1.10. The project stays above one, and the reserve can cover the shortfall to any covenant for a year while rents reset.

Step 5: the table

StrategyCoverage todayCoverage severeNormal-year cash, dollars
A, unhedged dollar1.430.951,500,000
B, local currency1.321.321,200,000
C, dollar plus one-year hedge1.341.34 in year one, falling after1,190,000
D, half and half plus reserve1.371.10about 1,350,000

Strategy D's normal-year cash is 500,000,000 less 365,000,000, 135,000,000 local units, 1,350,000 dollars, before the cost of carrying the reserve. All figures are hypothetical and rounded; coverage thresholds and lending terms are commercial practice.

Step 6: reading the answer

Strategy A pays an extra 300,000 dollars a year over B in a normal year. In the severe year it breaches, puts the lender at 96 percent loan to value and can cost you the building. If you believe the severe case has even a small chance within the loan's life, A is the most expensive strategy on the page, because the loss it risks is total. B is the safest and cheapest to explain. D is the practical middle ground when local debt is scarce: it survives the severe case with a margin, keeps more income than B, and the reserve covers the reset period. C is useful only as a bridge while you arrange B or D.

Step 7: the break-even rate

One more number tells a lender a great deal. Under strategy A, at what exchange rate does coverage fall to 1.0? Income in dollars must equal 3,500,000, so 500,000,000 divided by the rate equals 3,500,000. The rate is about 143 local units per dollar, a fall of about 30 percent. Under strategy D, solve 500,000,000 equals 1,750,000 times the rate plus 190,000,000. The rate is about 177, a fall of about 44 percent. Strategy D can absorb a much larger fall before the project stops paying its debt.

Step 8: what the severe case does to the lender's covenant

Suppose the loan requires coverage of at least 1.20, tested quarterly, with distributions blocked below it. Strategy A, at 0.95, fails the covenant and fails to pay its debt in full. Strategy B, at 1.32, passes with room. Strategy D, at 1.10, pays its debt but fails the 1.20 covenant, so distributions are trapped. How much reserve would cure that for a year? Coverage of 1.20 on 452,500,000 local units of debt service requires 543,000,000 local units of income, 43,000,000 more than the project earns. At the severe rate that is about 287,000 dollars. A reserve of 1,000,000 dollars covers that gap for more than three years if the covenant permits reserve cash to count, which you must negotiate. Read your loan agreement to see whether it does.

Step 9: the questions for your advisers

Three questions follow from the table. To the lender: which covenants are tested in which currency, and can reserve cash count towards a covenant cure? To the hedge provider: what tenor is available, what collateral would a losing hedge require, and how is the hedge priced on rolling? To the local bank: what local currency lending is available, for how long, and at what reset terms? Verify every answer in writing before you rely on it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is presenting only the today column to your investors and lender. The control is to show every strategy at today's rate, at the severe rate and at its break-even rate, side by side.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner models a gradual fall, a few percent a year. Currency crises are rarely gradual. Model a single large fall within one year, with rents frozen.

Callback

In Week 42, Priya sized a project loan backward from the coverage covenant. Today you saw that in a cross-border project the coverage ratio has a hidden input, the exchange rate, and that the loan you can safely carry depends on which currency it is in.

Recap

Unhedged dollar debt earns most in a normal year and breaches in a severe one. Local currency debt earns less and survives. A short hedge buys time. A split with a reserve survives a much larger fall. Always compute the break-even rate.

Next: Roman, on The Room: the political-risk insurance underwriting call.
checklist: I model every financing strategy at today's rate and a severe rate.
My severe case is a single large fall within one year, with rents frozen.
I compute coverage, loan to value and cash after debt service for each strategy.
I compute the break-even exchange rate at which coverage reaches 1.0.
I know how long my hedge lasts and what happens when it rolls.
I size a currency reserve to cover the reset period.
I show investors and lenders all columns, not only today's.
head: Field checklist
speak: One hypothetical project earning 500,000,000 local units a year, 5,000,000 dollars at 100 to the dollar, borrowing the equivalent of 40,000,000 dollars. Unhedged dollar debt gives coverage of about 1.43 today and about 0.95 if the currency falls to 150, with loan to value jumping to 96 percent. Local currency debt gives about 1.32 in both cases, because income and debt move together. A one-year hedge at about 106.7 locks coverage near 1.34 for one year, then the problem returns. Half dollar and half local debt with a reserve gives 1.37 today and about 1.10 in the severe case. Then the break-even: unhedged, coverage hits 1.0 at about 143 units, a 30 percent fall; split, at about 177, a 44 percent fall. The unhedged loan earns 300,000 dollars a year more in a normal year and risks the whole building in a bad one. I show every column.
terms: Severe case — a deliberately harsh but plausible scenario, here a single large currency fall within a year with rents frozen.
Break-even exchange rate — the rate at which coverage falls to 1.0, so income exactly covers debt service.
Currency reserve — cash held, often in the debt's currency, to cover debt service shortfalls while income adjusts after a devaluation.

hostile.q: Your split structure costs your investors 150,000 dollars a year against all-dollar debt. Why should they accept less?
hostile.a: Because the all-dollar structure breaches at about a 30 percent fall and the split survives to about 44 percent. In this currency's history, falls of that size within a year are plausible over a fifteen-year loan. The 150,000 dollars a year is the premium for not handing the building to the lender in that year. I have shown the investors both columns and the break-even rates, and the decision is theirs to make with the numbers in front of them.

title: The Political-Risk Insurance Underwriting Call
summary: A political-risk underwriter wants to know whether your investment is genuine, legal, well structured and worth insuring, and whether you will behave well if something goes wrong. Learn the lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind each question and how to hold your state when the questions turn to the government.
body:
A political-risk underwriter is pricing two things at once: what the host government might do, and what you might do. The second is the part you control, and your answers on the call are how the underwriter measures it.

Recall

Q. Under unhedged dollar debt in the worked example, at what exchange rate did coverage reach 1.0?

A. At about 143 local units per dollar, a fall of about 30 percent from 100.

Q. What is a pre-sale threshold, and who sets it?

A. A minimum level of binding sales a construction lender requires before funding, set by the lender as commercial practice, loan by loan.

Q. Why should board approval of a major decision be recorded in a resolution?

A. Because the resolution is the evidence that the company made the decision through its proper process, which protects directors and satisfies lenders, auditors and counterparties.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, I have sat with underwriters. They decline more applications for what the investor reveals about himself than for what the country might do. A policy is a long relationship: if a claim arises, the insurer will rely on your records, your cooperation and your conduct. The call is the first evidence of all three.

The scene

A hypothetical 15,000,000 dollar equity investment in a residential project abroad, through a holding company. You are applying for cover against inconvertibility and transfer restriction, expropriation and political violence for 10 years. On the call: an underwriter and a claims specialist from the insurer, and your broker. After the introductions the underwriter asks: "Walk me through how your money got into the country and how you expect it to come out."

The question behind the question

The surface question is about mechanics. The real questions are three. Was the investment made legally, with every registration and approval in place? Is the structure genuine, or built to manufacture coverage? And if transfers stop, will the insurer be able to prove what you were entitled to send? An underwriter knows that a claim is only as good as the documents behind it.

The lines to say

Start with the path. "The equity came from our holding company's bank account in two tranches, through a licensed bank, with the central bank registration filed on arrival. Here are the transfer confirmations and the registration certificates."

Then the way out. "Distributions will leave as dividends after local tax, through the same bank. We have the bank's written list of documents it needs for each outgoing payment, and our first test transfer cleared in five working days."

Then the structure, plainly. "The holding company was formed before we signed for the land, for financing and governance reasons recorded at the time. It has its own directors and bank account."

Then the honest risk. "Our biggest concern is a period of restricted transfers rather than seizure. We have local currency debt, so the project itself can keep paying its loan; what we want covered is our ability to bring distributions home."

Say that out loud now.

In legally, documented, out through a tested path, and here is the risk I actually want covered.

The lines never to say

Never say "we have good relationships with the minister, so expropriation will not happen." It suggests either that you are underestimating the risk or that you rely on relationships the insurer cannot underwrite, and it may raise questions about integrity. Never criticise the host government's politics on the call; an insurer working with that government on recoveries will not welcome a policyholder who has. Never say "we can sort out the registration later." Never imply that you want cover against the currency falling; the underwriter will hear that you do not understand the product.

When to stay silent

When the claims specialist asks what you would do if transfers stopped, give your plan and then stop. Do not fill the silence with reassurance. The specialist is weighing whether you would mitigate the loss and cooperate, and a short, concrete answer is stronger than a long, hopeful one.

Holding your state

Questions about corruption, sanctions and source of funds can feel personal. They are routine for every applicant. Answer them in the same tone as a question about the size of the building. If a question surprises you, say "I will confirm that in writing by Friday" and do so.

Worked examples: two answers to the same question

The underwriter asks: "What happens to the project if the government freezes rents?" Weak answer: "That would be very unfair, and I do not think they would." Strong answer: "We tested it. With local currency debt and our current operating costs, the project covers debt service for 18 months with rents frozen, using the reserve. A rent freeze alone is not an expropriation under the policy wording as we read it, so we have not asked you to cover it; we manage it in the structure." The second answer shows that you know where the policy stops.

A second example. The claims specialist asks: "Who keeps your records?" Weak: "Our accountant." Strong: "Our controller keeps a transfer file for every inbound and outbound payment, with the bank confirmation, the central bank filing and the board resolution, and it is backed up outside the country." Records held only inside the host country can be lost in exactly the event you are insuring against.

Closing the call

End by confirming what the underwriter still needs, in a list, and the date you will send it. "You need the second registration certificate, the board resolution approving the investment and the bank's written transfer requirements. You will have all three by Friday." Then ask: "Is there anything in our structure that would make a claim harder to pay, that we could fix now?" That question tells the underwriter you are thinking about the day of the claim, which is the day the policy exists for, and it often surfaces a condition you can meet cheaply before the policy is issued rather than argue about afterwards.

Monthly thread: cultural intelligence across Canada and Guyana

Cultural intelligence is the skill of reading what a room expects without abandoning your own standards. In general terms, and individuals vary widely, Canadian business practice often leans on written process, direct questions and decisions recorded in documents. Guyanese business practice, also in general terms, often places more weight on personal introductions, established relationships and respect for seniority, and on patience with how decisions move through institutions. Neither is better. A developer working across both learns to build the relationship and keep the written record.

The trap is to confuse relationship with influence. Building trust with officials and partners is good practice everywhere; seeking or offering anything that bends a decision is corruption everywhere, and it destroys both your insurance and your reputation. Ask yourself, Mr Shabazz, how you would explain each relationship to an underwriter, and whether you would be comfortable doing so.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a gap in the investment's paper trail that the insurer discovers only when you claim. The control is a transfer file, complete before the call and kept current for the life of the policy.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats the underwriting call as a sales pitch for the country. The underwriter knows the country. The call is about you.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught how to use professionals, including how to brief them in writing and challenge their advice. Your broker is a professional too. Brief the broker in writing before the call on the risks you want covered and those you do not, so the broker can steer the underwriter's questions towards your real exposure.

Recap

The underwriter prices the government and you. Show a legal, documented path in and a tested path out, a genuine structure and the specific risk you want covered. Never lean on political relationships, criticise the government or ask for cover against depreciation. Keep a transfer file outside the country.

Next: Kema, on Quiz and Recap: six questions on currency, convertibility, treaties and insurance.
checklist: I can show how the equity entered the country, with bank confirmations and registrations.
I have tested the outgoing transfer path and hold the bank's document list in writing.
I can explain why and when the holding structure was formed.
I know which risks I want covered and which I manage in the structure.
I keep a transfer file, backed up outside the host country.
I answer source-of-funds and integrity questions in a routine tone.
I never rely on political relationships as a risk control.
I briefed my broker in writing before the call.
head: Field checklist
speak: A political-risk underwriter prices two things: what the host government might do and what I might do. The question behind the questions is whether my investment is legal, whether my structure is genuine, and whether my records would support a claim. So I show the path in: bank confirmations and the central bank registration. The path out: dividends through the same bank, with its written document list and a test transfer that cleared. The structure: formed before the land deal, for recorded business reasons. And the risk I actually want covered: restricted transfers of my distributions, because local currency debt already protects the project. I never say a good relationship with a minister protects me, never criticise the government, and never ask for cover against the currency falling, because the policy does not do that. I keep a transfer file backed up outside the country, because that is the evidence a claim depends on.
terms: Underwriting — the insurer's assessment of a risk, deciding whether to cover it and on what terms and price.
Waiting period — the length of time a covered event must continue before the insurer pays a claim.
Transfer file — the record of every inbound and outbound investment payment, with bank confirmations, registrations and approvals.

hostile.q: If transfers stop, what will you do in the first ninety days, before our waiting period ends?
hostile.a: Notify you immediately in writing, apply through the bank and the central bank for every permitted transfer and keep the refusals, keep the project paying its local currency debt from local income, and hold distributions in a segregated local account so the amount blocked is clear. I will not use informal exchange channels, and I will not sign anything with the authorities that waives rights without your consent. You will have a monthly log from day one.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 43 Review: Currency, Convertibility, Treaties and Insurance
summary: Six questions test the week: the five country risks, the three hits of a devaluation, the price of a hedge, what political-risk insurance covers, the three layers of protection and Rule 43. A Red Pen drill on a hypothetical financing memo and a two-minute boardroom drill complete it.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: across a border, the country is a party to your deal, so you decide in advance which currency you earn and owe in, and who carries each risk the state could create.

Recall

Q. What is a transfer file, and why keep it outside the host country?

A. The record of every inbound and outbound investment payment with its confirmations and approvals. It is kept outside the country because records inside it can be lost in the very event you are insured against.

Q. What does the security package in a project loan cover?

A. Typically a mortgage over the land and building, a pledge over the SPV's shares, security over its bank accounts, and assignments of its key contracts and insurance proceeds.

Q. What is the difference between a corporation and a partnership as a vehicle, in general terms?

A. A corporation is a separate legal person whose owners' liability is usually limited and which may be taxed itself. A partnership is often a flow-through for tax, and general partners can be personally liable. Specific rules vary by jurisdiction.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, country risk is the subject most investors understand only after a crisis. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can sit with a lender, an insurer or a partner and say exactly where the cross-border risk sits. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Name the five country risks.

Answer: Currency mismatch, convertibility, transfer, expropriation, and political violence or breach of contract by the state. The first is a market risk; the other four are political.

Question 2. What three hits does a devaluation cause to a project with foreign-currency debt?

Answer: Lower coverage, higher loan to value in the lender's currency, and a lower return in the investor's home currency.

Question 3. What does a currency hedge cost, and what is its main limit?

Answer: Roughly the interest rate difference between the two currencies, which is about what you saved by borrowing in the cheaper one. Its main limit in smaller currencies is short tenor, and it may require posting collateral.

Question 4. What does political-risk insurance cover, and what does it not?

Answer: It covers inconvertibility, transfer restriction, expropriation, political violence and sometimes a state's breach of contract. It does not cover ordinary currency depreciation, and it carries waiting periods and exclusions.

Question 5. Name the three layers of legal protection and the weakness of each.

Answer: Domestic law, which can be amended; contracts with the state, which the state can breach; and treaties between states, which protect only qualifying investors and are enforced slowly through arbitration.

Question 6. What is Rule 43?

Answer: Never borrow in a currency your project does not earn unless the mismatch is hedged or reserved against, sized to survive a severe devaluation, and approved in writing as a deliberate decision, because a peg is a policy and policies end.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Roman framed the five country risks and the three tools: match, hedge and insure. Ford and Roman took Argentina's 2001 to 2002 convertibility collapse, where currency, convertibility and contract risk arrived together, giving Rule 43. Roman priced the three hits, the hedge and the insurance. REGA mapped the three layers of protection and compared Canada and Guyana in general terms. Roman worked a currency stress across four strategies. Roman then ran the underwriting call.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical investment committee memo and find the defects before reading on.

Financing recommendation. We recommend a 40,000,000 dollar loan in United States dollars at 7 percent, against local currency loans at 12 percent, saving about 2,000,000 dollars a year. The local currency has been stable for nine years and the central bank has stated its commitment to stability, so currency risk is low. To be prudent, we will buy political-risk insurance, which protects us against currency movements. Our coverage ratio of 1.45 gives ample headroom. Rents are in local currency and the leases have no indexation. Any hedging can be arranged after closing if needed.

The defects. First, the saving is presented as profit, when it is largely the market's price for the currency risk the memo then calls low. Second, nine years of stability and a central bank statement are evidence that a policy is working, not that it is permanent; Rule 43. Third, political-risk insurance does not cover currency movements; the memo misunderstands the product it relies on. Fourth, coverage of 1.45 is stated only at today's rate; there is no severe case and no break-even rate, so the headroom is untested. Fifth, rents in local currency with no indexation are a full currency mismatch with no natural offset. Sixth, deferring hedging until after closing leaves the project exposed from day one and may find the hedge unavailable or dearer once the market is under strain. A memo that names a risk and then dismisses it in the same paragraph is asking to be approved, not analysed.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a partner who asks: "The dollar loan is cheaper. Why are we not taking it?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "Because our rents are in local currency, and the dollar loan's lower rate is the price of the currency risk we would be taking. If the local currency fell by a third, which has happened in many countries within a single year, our coverage would drop from about 1.4 to below one and our loan to value in dollars would go above 90 percent. The lender would act, and we could lose the building. A hedge would cost roughly the interest difference, so the saving mostly disappears, and in this currency hedges run only a year or two. Insurance protects us if we cannot convert or transfer money, or if the state takes the asset, but not against the rate falling. So we are taking half the debt in local currency, keeping a currency reserve, and insuring our distributions against transfer restrictions. We earn a little less in a normal year, and we survive a bad one."

Notice that the model answer never uses the words convertibility, subrogation or covered interest parity. A partner needs the consequence: what happens to coverage, what the lender does, what the hedge and the insurance can and cannot fix, and what the structure costs in a normal year. Keep the vocabulary for the term sheet and the policy wording, and keep the consequences for the room.

Score your answer. Did you lead with the mismatch? Did you give one number for the severe case? Did you explain why hedging and insurance do not simply solve it? Did you finish inside two minutes? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a structure that looks protected because it has a hedge, an insurance policy and a treaty, when none of them covers the risk that actually hurts. The control is a protection map that matches each risk to the tool that covers it and names the gaps.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking of country risk as a single number, such as a country rating. It is five different risks, each with its own tool and its own gap.

Callback

In Week 42, Ford and Roman took Carillion, where risk passed down a contract became a credit risk on the party that accepted it. A dollar loan does the same thing across a border: the currency risk does not vanish because the lender is foreign; it lands on the borrower whose income is local.

Recap

Five country risks, three tools, three layers of protection. A devaluation hits coverage, loan to value and return. Hedges cost the interest difference and run short. Insurance covers acts of the state, not the rate. Rule 43 makes any mismatch deliberate, sized and approved.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, country risk. Across a border, five things can go wrong because of where the project is: currency mismatch, convertibility, transfer, expropriation, and political violence or a state breaking its contract. Three tools manage them: match the currency of debt to the currency of income, hedge what I cannot match, and insure the political risks. A devaluation hits three times: coverage falls, loan to value in the lender's currency rises, and my home-currency return shrinks. A hedge costs roughly the interest rate difference and in small currencies runs only a year or two. Political-risk insurance covers acts of the state, not a falling rate. Legal protection comes in three layers, domestic law, contracts with the state and treaties, each weaker or slower than it looks. Argentina's peg showed that a policy can end in weeks. Rule 43: no currency mismatch unless it is hedged or reserved, sized to survive a severe fall, and approved in writing.
terms: Country risk — the risks an investment faces because of the country it is in, rather than the project itself.
Protection map — a table matching each risk to the tool or legal layer that covers it, its conditions and its gaps.
Natural hedge — matching the currency of income and obligations so exchange rate moves affect both equally.

hostile.q: You have a hedge, an insurance policy and a treaty. Surely that covers everything?
hostile.a: No, and I have mapped exactly what each covers. The hedge covers this year's exchange rate, not the rest of the loan. The insurance covers our inability to convert or transfer, and seizure, not a falling rate. The treaty gives us a claim that could take years. The largest remaining gap is a severe devaluation in years two to fifteen, so half our debt is in local currency and we hold a reserve. That is the part of the structure doing most of the work.
